vocabulary.note: Works for hello AND goodbye — but only with people you're on informal terms with. Saying it to a stranger is... a choice.

vocabulary.exEn: Good evening, a table for two?

vocabulary.note: You say this when going to bed — NOT to greet someone at 9pm. Greeting with it marks you as a tourist faster than socks with sandals.
The social safety net. Not too stiff, not too familiar. Perfect with strangers. Italians use it constantly; textbooks teach it rarely.
With strangers or elders: “come sta?”. Getting the formal/informal choice right earns silent respect.
A touch more honest and very common: “non c'è male” — not bad, can't complain.

vocabulary.exEn: Thanks a million for the help!

vocabulary.note: The multi-tool of Italian: you're welcome, come in, after you, help yourself. One word, four situations, zero stress.
Polite alternative: “per piacere”. Both make you sound raised right.
Scusa with friends, scusi with everyone else. Also how you get a waiter's attention without shouting.

vocabulary.exEn: Nice to meet you, my name is Marco.

vocabulary.note: Uno loses its -o before a noun: un cane, un amico — never “uno cane”. You're welcome.
Identical to “sei” = you are. Context saves you: “sei anni” (six years) vs “sei simpatico” (you're nice).
In Italy 13 is just a number. The unlucky one is 17, diciassette. Blame Roman numerals (XVII → VIXI, “I lived”).
Italians use the 24-hour clock: 15:00 = quindici. Miss a train appointment once and you'll never forget.
Dieci drops its last vowel: diciotto, NOT “dieciotto”. Same for diciannove.
Venti + uno → ventuno. The -i falls off before uno and otto: ventotto, not “ventiotto”.
Plural is “mila”: duemila, tremila. A thousand little irregularities, this language.
Bread arrives unasked — and often with “il coperto”, a small cover charge. Check the menu, not the vibes.
Ordering water: “naturale” (still) or “frizzante” (sparkling). Tap water isn't a thing — that's “acqua del rubinetto”, and brace yourself.
“Un caffè” means espresso. If you want the big watery thing, ask for “un caffè americano” and endure the look you'll get.
A breakfast drink ONLY. Order one after lunch and the barista will still serve it — while quietly filing you under “tourist” forever.

vocabulary.ex: La pasta fatta in casa è la migliore.

vocabulary.note: Ananas sulla pizza: technically legal, morally contested. Your nonna's opinion is stronger than any law.
Asking for parmigiano on a fish pasta is considered a small act of war. Don't.
Rosso o bianco? House wine (“della casa”) is often the honest choice, and cheap.
Order “un cono” (cone) or “una coppetta” (cup). If it's florescent green pistachio, run — real pistachio is dull beige and delicious.
Say it loudly enough and someone will eventually come. Splitting the bill exists, but expect the waiter's quiet judgement.
To call them: “scusi!” works. Snapping your fingers does too — if you want to become the village's main character.
Italian breakfast is sweet: cappuccino + cornetto. Eggs at 8am will get you looks of pure anthropological curiosity.
The verb you'll conjugate 200 times a day. “Sono stanco” — I'm tired. You'll be saying that a lot too, presumably.
Fair warning: Italians use fare for everything — fare colazione, fare una passeggiata, fare tardi. It carries the whole language on its back.
“Andiamo!” alone means “let's go!” or an enthusiastic “come on!”. You'll use it more than you think.
Irregular: io vengo, tu vieni, loro vengono. Not “veno” — that's not a word, it's a cry for help.
Io bevo, tu bevi. Asking “vuoi bere qualcosa?” is the classic Italian move to extend an evening.
The magic polite form: “vorrei” (I would like). “Voglio” is blunt; “vorrei” opens doors, menus, and hearts.
“Posso...?” is your golden key for any request. No Italian sentence survives without it, roughly.
The polite escape hatch from any conversation: “Devo scappare!” — I must run! Nobody knows where. It doesn't matter.
Sapere = facts & skills; conoscere = people & places. You “sai” the answer, you “conosci” Marco. Mixing them up is endearing. Once.

vocabulary.en: good luck (lit: into the wolf's mouth)
vocabulary.ex: Domani ho l'esame. — In bocca al lupo!
vocabulary.exEn: Tomorrow I have my exam. — Good luck!
vocabulary.note: Never answer “grazie” — it cancels the luck. The correct reply is “crepi!” (may it die). Yes, you're wishing death on the wolf. It's tradition.

vocabulary.en: what a drag! / so annoying (mildly rude)
vocabulary.note: Literally “what balls”. Rude-ish but extremely common — about bureaucracy, delays, Mondays. Calibrate your audience.

vocabulary.ex: Non esco stasera, sono al verde.
vocabulary.exEn: I'm not going out tonight, I'm broke.
vocabulary.note: Likely from old gambling tables — when your money was gone, you were “at the green”. Very relatable after payday week.
A complete sentence. A philosophy. The most honest word in Italian: shoulders optional but recommended.

vocabulary.exEn: Are we going to Sicily this summer? — I wish!
vocabulary.note: As an answer, magari means “I wish”. Alone in a sentence, it means “maybe”. Same word, opposite moods. Italian!

vocabulary.exEn: I can't wait to see you.
vocabulary.note: Literally “I don't see the hour”. Follow with “di” + infinitive or “di” + noun. Deploy liberally before holidays.

vocabulary.exEn: Thanks for the ride! — Don't mention it!
vocabulary.note: Also used sarcastically: “Figurati se mi chiama” = “as if he'd ever call me”. Tone does all the work.
The most versatile syllable in Italy. Encouragement, disbelief, pleading — context and eyebrow position required.

vocabulary.ex: Hai visto il bagno? Che schifo!
vocabulary.exEn: Did you see the bathroom? Gross!

vocabulary.en: to embarrass yourself / make a bad impression
vocabulary.ex: Ho fatto una figuraccia al colloquio.
vocabulary.exEn: I made a fool of myself at the interview.
vocabulary.note: Fear of this motivates half of all Italian social behaviour. The other half is espresso.
“Mi piaci” is the flirt. “Ti piaccio?” is fishing. Both work; one is braver.
The ending depends on WHO you're complimenting, not who's speaking. Get it wrong and the compliment gets... creative.

vocabulary.en: can I buy you a coffee?
vocabulary.ex: Posso offrirti un caffè, se hai cinque minuti.
vocabulary.exEn: I can buy you a coffee, if you have five minutes.
vocabulary.note: The most Italian flirting strategy ever: reasonable, caffeinated, and hard to refuse.

vocabulary.ex: Mi dai il tuo numero? Ci sentiamo.
vocabulary.exEn: Can I get your number? We'll talk.

vocabulary.en: are you free tonight? (to a woman)
vocabulary.note: To a man: “sei libero stasera?”. Follow-up you'll need: “ti va di uscire?” — do you feel like going out?

vocabulary.en: I'd like to invite you to dinner
vocabulary.exEn: I'd like to invite you to dinner, Saturday.
vocabulary.note: Notice the conditional “vorrei” — politeness even at maximum flirt. That's the Italian way.
Literally “you are missing TO me”. The grammar is doing the emotional heavy lifting here, as Italian grammar does.

vocabulary.en: I care about you / I love you (affection)
vocabulary.note: For friends, family, and slow-burn romances. NOT to be confused with “ti amo” — that one's heavy artillery.
Reserved. Powerful. Telling it to your barista will end your coffee privileges. Use accordingly.
Practice this one carefully. There may be a quiz later, in one sense or another.

vocabulary.it: ci conosciamo? No? Allora diamoci del tu.
vocabulary.en: do we know each other? No? Then let's switch to informal you.
vocabulary.note: A classic cheeky opener. Cheesy rating: gorgonzola. Success rate: unverifiable, but it gets a laugh, which is half the battle.

vocabulary.it: sei stanca? Hai corso nella mia testa tutto il giorno.
vocabulary.en: are you tired? You've been running through my head all day.
vocabulary.note: The translated classic pickup line. Deploy at your own risk. Warning label not included.

vocabulary.it: sei del pane? Perché mi hai lievitato il cuore.
vocabulary.en: are you bread? Because you made my heart rise.
vocabulary.note: For bread enthusiasts only. Worst-case scenario: you get bread out of the conversation. That's not nothing.
The adjective matches YOUR gender, not the listener's. Ending in -o if you're male, -a if you're female. Democracy in grammar form.
Adjectives in -ese are gender-neutral: inglese, francese, belga-style peace of mind. One ending, zero drama.
The proper adjective for the country is “statunitense”, but real people say “americano”. Fight us, geographers.
Same ending for both genders — Belgium gives you three languages and one easy adjective. Fair trade.
Careful: “olandese” is from Holland. The whole country is “i Paesi Bassi”. Dutch people appreciate the distinction. A bit.
Formal version: “Di dov'è, Lei?”. Answer with “Sono di...” + city. No article, no stress.
For countries instead of cities: “Vengo dalla Francia” (from France), “Vivo in Italia” (I live in Italy). Prepositions are the final boss of Italian.
Country names love articles: l'Italia, la Francia, il Belgio. But with “in” the article vanishes: “Vivo in Italia”. Grammar has trust issues.
Yes, the article is mandatory: “il Belgio”, not just “Belgio”. Tiny country, tiny rules.
Plural country, plural everything: “Sono andato negli Stati Uniti”. Even the preposition gets complicated. Very American.
A Brit is “britannico” — a precise, slightly formal word. “Inglese” is the everyday shortcut, the Welsh forgive no one.

vocabulary.exEn: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you repeat?

vocabulary.note: Formal: “come, scusi?”. The Italian way of saying “I heard you, I just refuse to process it”.

vocabulary.exEn: How do you say “laptop” in Italian?
vocabulary.note: The single most useful question in any language class. Italians will answer with joy — we love explaining Italian. Sometimes too much.
Literally “what does it want to say” — yes, words have opinions in Italian. Polite twin: “cosa significa?”.
Formal: “può ripetere?”. You will need this. Everyone needs this. Even natives use it when grandpa mumbles.
Italians speak fast with their hands full. This phrase is a survival skill, not a weakness.
Formal: “Lei come si chiama?”. The book drills this for a reason — introductions open every door in Italy.
Pair it with “boh!” from Modi di dire for maximum Italian effect. Shrugging is not required but strongly encouraged.
Always feminine, like “informazione” and “attenzione”. Nouns in -zione are feminine without exception — one rule Italy actually keeps.
“I compiti” — always plural, like the sighing that accompanies them. “Devo fare i compiti” = I have to do my homework.
